coverage: 29 sources fetched raw and read, 21 substantive, 52 claims, every non-empty quotation re-checked against the fetched text before writing. ROSTER: the angle named no individual titles, so the roster was built from the two standing bibliographies — BrightWeavings' "Professional Scholarship" (20 items) and "Student Papers" (17 items) — plus OpenAlex (80 hits on "Guy Gavriel Kay", two pages walked), Crossref bibliographic queries, and the Wikipedia relay. FETCHED: Randall (Canadian Literature 129, 1991), Webb x2, Gunn (Easton Press intro), Cobb (Foundation 2005), Ordway (1998), Malosse (Anabases 5, 2007, English and French), Ringel (ICFA 2009), Patton (Sarantine Letters, in-world conceit), Doherty, Cawsey (Arthuriana 25.2, PDF), Taylor, Clements, Rettino (McGill honours 2012), Töyrylä (Helsinki BA 2017), Hatch (Calgary), Kleander (Stirling 2008), Campbell (Wollongong PhD 2013, via a Figshare mirror after the repository blocked the download), Pugar (Zagreb, Words to Works), Doshlova (Kuban/UrFU, Russian), Thompson's 1989 Camelot Project interview, the Locus 2025 interview, the LARB 2016 interview, and the Wikipedia articles on Kay and Tigana. ABSTRACT ONLY: Johnston (Palgrave 2019, read raw from a Wayback capture of the SpringerLink page) and Borowska-Szerszun (Orbis Litterarum 2026, read from the Crossref record). BLOCKED: Gary K. Wolfe, "Guy Gavriel Kay: An Introduction", Journal of the Fantastic in the Arts 20.2 (2009) — the JSTOR issue page fails to render and its only other index, Questia, is defunct with no Wayback capture; Toswell, "Guy Gavriel Kay: Historical Fantasy" (Amsterdam UP / De Gruyter Brill 2025) and Borowska-Szerszun, "Remembering the Romance" (Boydell 2020) — publisher pages return empty bodies, the books are not in OAPEN or DOAB, and the Google Books API quota was exhausted; Borowska-Szerszun, "When Gods are Absent from Fantasy" (2017) — the Białystok repository PDF is a 4.7 MB image-only scan yielding 18 characters; Anabases on OpenEdition — Anubis bot filter, no Wayback capture (cured by the author-authorized reprint). ROUTES: 19 substantive by live raw HTML, 3 by PDF binary plus text extraction (one only via a Figshare mirror), 2 by abstract records (Wayback and Crossref). NEGATIVE FINDING: no stylometric, corpus-stylistic or computational study of Kay exists that OpenAlex, Crossref or open web search surfaced — every quantitative claim in this angle is a hand count by a narratologist (Randall's 26 focalizants and 87 shifts; Kleander's 21 focalizants and more than 150 focalizations in Tigana). The web-search quota was exhausted mid-sweep, so the last expansion rounds ran through OpenAlex, Crossref and bibliography chasing only; two consecutive index queries surfaced nothing new.

claims.claim: Randall states that in the passage narrating Darien's death in The Darkest Road the sentences are short and the description concrete.
claims.source: Neil Randall, critic, Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991)
claims.quote: Sentences are short, description is concrete.

claims.claim: Randall describes the tone of that same Darien death passage as matter-of-fact.
claims.source: Neil Randall, critic, Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991)
claims.quote: The tone, moreover, is matter-of-fact.

claims.claim: Randall reads the passage narrating the departure of Arthur, Lancelot and Guinevere as a deliberate reach for rhetorical high style, in contrast with the plain Darien passage.
claims.source: Neil Randall, critic, Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991)
claims.quote: the language here is an obvious attempt at rhetorical

claims.claim: Randall explains the elevated register of the Arthurian departure scene as a consequence of who perceives it, not of the event's importance.
claims.source: Neil Randall, critic, Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991)
claims.quote: because it is perceived by minds capable of comprehending magnificence

claims.claim: Randall counts twenty-six different agents of focalization in The Fionavar Tapestry.
claims.source: Neil Randall, critic, Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991)
claims.quote: employs twenty-six different agents of focalization
claims.page: opening section, before 'Assimilating the Secondary World'

claims.claim: Randall counts twenty-one shifts of focalization in the eighth chapter of The Summer Tree.
claims.source: Neil Randall, critic, Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991)
claims.quote: shifts focalization twenty-one times

claims.claim: Randall counts eighty-seven shifts of focalization across Darien's search for Rakoth, with Darien himself the focalizant only nine of those times.
claims.source: Neil Randall, critic, Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991)
claims.quote: the narrative shifts focalization eighty-seven times

claims.claim: Randall argues that Kay's shifts of focalization delay the unfolding of the story as well as advancing it.
claims.source: Neil Randall, critic, Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991)
claims.quote: the shifts delay the unfolding of the story

claims.claim: Randall argues the reader must assemble Kay's secondary world by inference from the successive focalizations rather than from direct exposition.
claims.source: Neil Randall, critic, Canadian Literature 129 (Summer 1991)
claims.quote: Our task is to piece together the world by understanding the focalizations.
